title: Volvo's big batteries: We drive its updated 2028 plug-in hybrids
text:
Volvo provided flights from Washington, DC, to Copenhagen, Denmark, and accommodation so Ars could drive the XC60 and XC90 plug-in hybrids. Ars does not accept paid editorial content. 
 COPENHAGEN, Denmark—If we lived in the world that Volvo’s product planners expected back when the current XC90  debuted in 2015 , both it and the smaller but related  XC60  (which arrived in 2017) might have been the last of their kind as  everything went electric . As we know, the future hasn’t turned out quite like that, especially in  the critically important US market . At the same time, Europe and China  are  electrifying, which seems like an argument against spending resources on developing all-new replacements for models that might not have an eight-year lifespan in most markets. 
 So instead, Volvo has given the XC60 and XC90 another lifecycle refresh. The exterior styling tweaks are minimal; the bigger three-row XC90 had already been given a new look last year, and the XC60 now gains a similar grille and the same matrix headlights, for instance. And that’s no bad thing—both were, and remain, handsome shapes that are popular with Volvo’s customer base. 
 Instead, the Swedish automaker’s attention has been on bringing the technology up to date for model year 2028 standards. Which means a much bigger battery for the PHEVs, with sufficient capacity for a couple of days of daily driving for most of us before needing to be recharged. There’s also new, modern infotainment and interiors that are now even nicer to spend time in than before.   Read full article

title: Ford unveils the GT41 as it hopes to win Le Mans again
text:
Sixty years ago, after two failed attempts, Ford won the 24 Hours of Le Mans with its GT40 race car. In the years since, the Blue Oval has been back to France more than a few times, with varying success. It could never replicate the GT40’s success winning overall, but it celebrated the 40th anniversary  with a class win . Now it wants another shot at the  really big trophy , and it debuted the car during the Detroit Lions-Chicago Bears football game today: meet the GT41. 
 “Revealing the Ford GT41 is a significant moment for everyone involved in this program,” said Dan Sayers, manager of Ford Racing’s Hypercar program. “It's the result of an enormous amount of work across our engineering, design, and development teams and an important milestone on our journey towards 2027. We know the scale of the challenge ahead—the level of competition in Hypercar is incredibly high, and there are no shortcuts to success. Our focus has been on building the right foundations, bringing together the right people and making sure we learn as much as possible from every stage of development.”

title: Synthetic controls meet Lucas! Unifying causal effects and structural decompositions
text: This paper merges two large literatures in macroeconomics, Synthetic Control Method (SCM) and Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium (DSGE) models, into a single framework. SCM effectively estimates causal treatment effects but lacks insights into underlying economic mechanisms, and it does not offer a framework for policy analysis: its estimated effect is a reduced-form object that shifts with the policy regime, leaving it exposed to the Lucas critique. By integrating SCM outcomes into a micro-founded DSGE framework, representing the treatment as an observable event that loads on the model’s structural shocks, we identify the transmission channels underlying the SCM-estimated treatment effects and enhance structural interpretation. Our approach recovers policy-invariant structural primitives rather than the regime-dependent gap, enabling counterfactual policy analysis that is robust to the Lucas critique. It thereby unites the empirical transparency of synthetic controls with the structural discipline of DSGE models – two complementary literatures that have long developed in isolation.

title: Jensen Huang was gone for 11 days. That was Nvidia’s succession test, and the board failed it
text:
Jensen Huang’s return to  Nvidia  is being told as a comeback. The shares jumped about 30% on the news. The founder was back at his desk. Order restored. 



 I read it differently. Those 11 days were the first real test of whether Nvidia could function without the man who built it. The board failed that test, and the way it failed should worry directors at every company whose CEO looks irreplaceable. 



 The sequence of events tells a story. 



 On November 12,  Nvidia announced that its board had accepted Huang’s resignation , after reports about his private life and a foreign intelligence operation aimed at him. CFO Colette Kress became interim CEO. The board said it would consider internal and external candidates. 



 Five days later, on the earnings call, chair Harvey Jones told analysts the board did “not intend to reinstate Jensen.” 



 Then the alternatives fell away. The  Financial Times  reported that the board had approached Rene Haas, the Arm CEO who spent seven years at Nvidia. On November 23, Haas extended his contract at Arm through 2033. The same day,  Nvidia’s directors voted unanimously to bring Huang back, saying they had received input from senior levels of the U.S. government . Trump told CNBC that he made a personal assurance that sealed the decision. 



 The board’s own independent investigation is still open. The directors reinstated their CEO before their own inquiry had finished. 



 That’s the detail I can’t get past. A board that says no on a Tuesday and yes six days later has run out of options. 



 A CEO nobody can replace is a CEO nobody can refuse. 



 Accountability depends on a credible alternative. When a board has a successor ready, its questions carry weight, because everyone in the room knows the company survives if the answers fall short. When it has nobody, the CEO holds the leverage and both sides know it. The duty to oversee him turns into a duty to keep him. 



 Huang has run Nvidia since he co-founded it in 1993. The board had three decades to prepare for the day he wasn’t there. When that day came, it had a CFO doing two jobs, one outside name, and a market that wanted him back. Yale’s Jeffrey Sonnenfeld wrote in  Fortune  the board had no Plan B. 



 Investors made the same point from the other side. Within days of the resignation, prominent shareholders were urging the board to keep the door open to Huang. Nobody outside the company had the facts. What they were pricing was a business with no one else to run it. 



 The board has since created a national security committee and is hiring a chief compliance officer. Those are controls on conduct. Neither one is a successor. 



 I coach CEOs, and I’ve watched how boards arrive here. Nobody decides to skip succession. It gets postponed, one good quarter at a time. 



 Over the years a founder’s identity and the company’s fuse. Raising the question of who comes next starts to feel like disloyalty, so directors leave it for another meeting. The CEO rarely pushes either. Planning your own exit means picturing a company that no longer needs you, and that is the hardest thing to ask of someone whose whole identity is the company. 



 So both sides stay comfortable. The cost arrives on the one day the board needs a choice and finds it doesn’t have one. 



 Plenty of boards are living with the same arrangement right now, and it’s invisible for as long as the results are good. 



 Two tests will tell a director where their board stands. 



 First, name the person who could run the company on Monday. One name, already inside the building, whom the top team would follow. If the honest answer is the CFO as caretaker, you have a holding pattern. 



 Second, recall the last time the board said no to the CEO on something he cared about. If nobody can remember one, the board has already stopped overseeing him. It just hasn’t been tested yet. 



 Huang may prove to be the right leader for Nvidia’s next chapter. The investigation may answer every open question. Neither would change what the 11 days showed. 



 The board now enters the next crisis in a weaker position than the last one. It has shown its investors, its government and its CEO that it has no alternative to him. He knows it. So does everyone who will ever need to challenge him. 



 Every director reading this should ask the question Nvidia’s board had to answer in public. 



 If our CEO were gone tomorrow, would we have a choice?

title: I have a front-row seat to Norway’s cutting-edge AI newsroom experiment. Even with AI on more than 200 stories a day, a human still checks every one
text:
Every day, Norway’s largest newspaper, VG, asks an AI model to suggest a headline, search terms and other details for each of its roughly 200 new articles. Before a journalist sees anything, a second model checks the first. In October, across all the newsrooms that use the system, it rejected about one in six of the first model’s attempts. Then the journalist checks the suggestion, and so does an editor, depending on how the newsroom is set up. The cheapest checker goes first, and the people who answer for the story still go last. 



 “Keep a human in the loop” has become the standard answer to AI’s mistakes. I wanted to know what that human costs, so I asked three Norwegian news organizations what it takes, and whether that has gone up or down as the tools improved. What I learned is that the cost of a check depends heavily on who does it, and on how close that person is to the original work. 



 I direct a research center on media technology in Norway, where newsrooms began publishing AI-written summaries in 2023. The answers come from the AI Foundations unit at Schibsted Media, the group that owns VG and the regional daily Bergens Tidende; from an editor at Bergens Tidende; and from an editor at Fjell-Ljom, a small local paper in the mountain town of Røros. I am not a neutral observer here: Schibsted Media and Bergens Tidende are partners in my center and help fund it, and I am preparing a grant application with Fjell-Ljom. 



 Nobody had a measured figure, and the numbers that exist elsewhere come from surveys, not stopwatches. But in one newsroom I could set the check against the work it replaces. 



 Seconds, if you wrote the story 



 At Bergens Tidende, known as  BT , reporters publish 15 to 20 stories of their own a day. AI is not, for now, permitted to write them, but it does write a short version of the finished story, which the reporter is responsible for checking before an editor checks it too. Jan Stian Vold, BT’s development editor, estimates that a reporter who knows the story needs anything from a few seconds to a couple of minutes, and that the editor’s look adds a minute or two. Writing the short version by hand, he told me, takes a reporter three to five minutes. These are his estimates, not measurements. Still, for the person who wrote the story, checking the machine’s version takes less time than writing one. 



 Vold’s guess is that about one short version in ten needs a fix, and he says the summaries have kept improving with the models. The usual problem is clumsy grammar, or a summary that misses what the reporter considers the most important point. “Almost never hallucinations,” he wrote to me. As far as BT knows, it has never published a critical mistake this way. 



 Office workers describe something different. In a  Workday survey  of 3,200 employees who use AI at large companies, nearly 40% of the time AI saved was lost to rework. In a survey of 1,150 U.S. employees by  researchers at BetterUp and Stanford , each piece of workslop, AI-generated work that looks finished and is not, took nearly two hours to deal with. These are self-reports about longer documents, not a like-for-like comparison with a newsroom summary. But one difference stands out. In the office, the check often falls to someone who did not do the work and first has to find out what a right answer would look like. At BT, it falls to the one person who already knows. 



 A  Georgia Tech researcher argued this month  that catching AI’s mistakes is a mental burden that eats the gains. In the one newsroom where I could estimate it, the check took less time than the writing it replaced, and the reason is who does the checking. 



 Why two answers can both be right 



 Johanna Johansson, who works in AI Foundations at Schibsted Media, told me that “hallucinations are surprisingly common.” Vold had written “almost never.” Both can be right. She was speaking of AI-generated content in general, he of one narrow task, the summary of a text the reporter has just finished. Two things may be at work here, and I cannot separate them: a narrow task may produce fewer errors, and a checker who knows the material may spot the ones that remain faster. 



 On one point they agree. “Generally we always have a human in the loop,” Johansson said. That was always a firm principle, she said, and the huge improvements in the models have not made it any less important. 



 Checking as part of the work 



 Fjell-Ljom was named  Norway’s local newspaper of the year  in 2025 among papers with fewer than 4,000 subscribers. AI is involved in roughly one to three of its stories a day, which Iver Waldahl Lillegjære, its development editor, estimates is a third to half of everything it publishes. There is no separate AI check at the end. The checking is part of the work itself, so the journalist stays in control from start to finish, and the checking has stayed the same as the paper’s use of AI has grown. AI often gets things wrong, less often in the facts than in judgment calls a good journalist would have made differently. Most problems are caught along the way, though some can still get through, as in any journalism. Before it built this workflow, Lillegjære published 40 to 50 council summaries made with ChatGPT, and two minor factual errors got through. Readers spotted them, and they were corrected within about an hour. “A convincing answer is of little use if you don’t know how it came about,” he says. 



 A judgment call, I would add, is the kind of error that only someone who knows the story is likely to notice. 



 Better tools, the same check 



 So has the checking gone up or down? For BT’s newsroom as a whole, Vold could not say. His own work is administration and presentations, not journalism, and there his checking has gone down as he has learned to use AI as an assistant and not as a source of facts. At Fjell-Ljom it has stayed constant, because it was never a separate step. What nobody described is letting go of the check on what gets published. 



 I think they are right to hold that line, and the reason goes beyond the errors that remain. The check at BT is cheap because of everything the reporter did before the summary appeared. Hand the same summary to someone who had not reported the story, and the check would either take far longer or turn into a formality. A freelance journalist interviewed for a 2025  master’s thesis at Aalto University  made a similar point: typing out an interview word for word “really gets you inside it in a way that reading over a transcription and just checking for errors doesn’t.” 



 For companies outside the news business, I take three things from this. Count the check: how many items, how many people look at each one, and how many minutes each look takes. Then set that against what the task took before. Do not treat a falling error rate as permission to stop checking. Nobody I asked has. Above all, give the check to the person who knows the work, instead of adding a reviewer downstream who has to start from nothing. In these newsrooms, that is what keeps the check manageable. 



 As AI takes over more of what comes before the check, I would worry less about the minutes than about whether anyone is left who can tell in seconds that something is wrong.
